item.content:encoded:
The following article originally appeared on The Arize Blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission.

Every time you think you’ve just got the hang of this AI thing, another thing gets declared “dead.” This week, it’s agent harnesses.

Back in ancient history, aka June, I wrote a piece called “Frameworks are dying, harnesses are winning” and I don’t take that back. But this week a research team took a specialized agent harness, trained its behavior into a model and then took the harness away. The trained model handily beat the original model+harness combination. So are harnesses done now?

Betteridge’s Law applies, so the answer is “no.” But the job of the agent harness is changing. Parts of a harness that are sufficiently generalizable can be trained into the model. That leaves your harness holding the things that make your application unique: your tools, your data, your users, and your environment. You still have to build a harness, but you have to be prepared to regularly throw it away and rebuild it to keep up with evolving models.

This blog is about why that’s true, and how to turn “constantly rebuilding your harness” into an automatic process, not a giant time suck.

How Harness-Zero trained an agent harness into a model

First, the paper that kicked off this train of thought for me: it’s called “Harness-Zero,” from Haoran Ye and colleagues at Peking University. Its subject is harness distillation, i.e., training a model to reproduce behavior that used to be the result of the harness. The methodology is a little involved, so stick with me.

First, the team built a specialized harness for a small model, Qwen3.5-9B. An automated loop, run with Kimi K3, analyzed where the small model kept failing on training tasks and added the usual components to fix those failures: custom tools, middleware rules that block risky actions, skills files and memory. They called this the “evolved harness.”

Then they used that harness to generate training data. They put the small model through training tasks inside a minimal harness while a stronger model, GPT-5.6 Sol, reviewed every step the small model proposed. Sol used a copy of the evolved harness to tell it whether that step was a good idea. Sol passed good ideas from the small model through unchanged, and whenever the small model and the guidance disagreed, Sol made the smallest fix needed before the step ran.

That gave them a bunch of training runs and, crucially, data about what needed to be corrected. Then they created the distilled model: They fine-tuned the small model on the corrected runs. Then they removed the evolved harness, the reviewer, and everything else.

They then tested both the evolved harness and the distilled model head-to-head on spreadsheet editing, multi-app tool use, and chemistry. The distilled model’s average task success rose 21 points versus its untrained predecessor. That’s more than the untrained model gained with the full evolved harness attached. So the distilled model wasn’t just as good as the model+harness, it was noticeably better.

What harness distillation can and cannot move into the model

It’s not that the distilled model ran with no harness whatsoever: It still ran inside a minimal loop with one Bash tool, and the authors say that their method narrows what a harness has to provide rather than eliminating it entirely. The distilled model also didn’t win every competition: In chemistry, where the task is predicting which molecules combine to make a target compound, the distilled model trailed the harnessed version by eight points. The harness there supplied chemistry knowledge, candidate-generation logic, and a molecule validation tool. The authors’ explanation is that step-by-step procedures, like inspecting before editing and verifying before finishing, are much easier to train in than deep domain knowledge. Context management didn’t fully transfer either. So there are still some things harnesses definitely need to do.

Why training on corrected runs made the difference

But the most important finding, in my opinion, is that they showed what kind of training made the difference:

  • Fine-tuning on the stronger model’s own successful runs left the small model’s score exactly where it started. Just knowing somebody else is smarter isn’t enough.
  • So did fine-tuning on runs the small model completed inside the evolved harness. Again, all that teaches the model is “somebody is better than you at this.”
  • Giving the reviewer the correct answers produced nearly perfect training runs and a model that barely improved, this time because it overfit and learned nothing.
  • What worked was training on the corrected runs: The model was able to see runs that looked a lot like what it would have done, but with small changes still within its capacity.

Remember that part, because it’s going to be important.

Why models are absorbing parts of the agent harness

In Rich Sutton’s 2019 essay The Bitter Lesson, he looked back over 70 years of AI research and found the same pattern in chess, Go, speech recognition, and computer vision: Researchers built their own knowledge of the problem into their systems. That helped in the short term, then plateaued, and eventually lost by a wide margin to general methods, search and learning, that improve as computation gets cheaper.

A harness is that kind of built-in knowledge, and model training is the learning that ends up absorbing it. Sutton’s second point is also relevant: He argued we should build in “only the meta-methods that can find and capture this arbitrary complexity,” rather than the things we’ve already figured out. For harnesses that means: don’t just build it, but capture the process you used to build it, and automate that process.

But that’s a general prediction. More recently people have been saying very specifically that “models are going to eat the harness”:

  • In January, Jesus Rodriguez at TheSequence wrote “The Great Absorption,” arguing that hand-coded agent scaffolding keeps losing to capabilities models learn directly.
  • In February, Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, told Y Combinator that scaffolding might buy you 10% to 20% on a task, and then “the gain is wiped out with the next model.”
  • In March, Vivek Trivedy at LangChain predicted that planning, self-verification, and long-running coherence would move from the harness into the model.
  • And so did lots of other people, probably more than I’ve been able to find.

Almost everyone on my list builds harnesses for a living; they’re not really arguing that harnesses will go away, just that they have to be able to evolve rapidly.

What still belongs in an agent harness

As noted already, some types of knowledge don’t seem to transfer well from distillation. In ARC Prize’s results for ARC-AGI-3, Gemini 3.8 Flash scores 3.4-times higher with one harness than with another. The better harness keeps the model’s reasoning state between requests and compacts long conversations. That’s context management, one of the things Harness-Zero said they couldn’t fully train in.

Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 prompting guide, released this week, also shows evidence of shrinking harnesses. It suggests deleting “think carefully” instructions because the model now sets its own amount of thinking, and it tells you to retest scaffolding you built for charts and screenshots because the model reads them better without that help now. But at the same time, Anthropic added new harness pieces: a system prompt paragraph that keeps unattended agents from stopping early, a reminder your harness sends when a long run goes quiet, and elapsed-time budgets for multi-agent setups.

So harnesses aren’t going to shrink to nothing, but what’s in them is going to need to evolve with every new model generation, and the parts that survive are the ones tied to your specific tools, data, and environment.

How to evolve an agent harness as models improve

If your harness has to change every generation, the natural move is to automate the changes, but Google’s RRSI paper shows how that can go wrong. Unconstrained automatic harness evolution overfits, meaning the harness gets better at the tasks it’s tuned on without getting better at the general job. In their tests, the unconstrained version scored highest of any variant on the tasks it evolved against, and landed within a point of the original, unevolved harness on benchmarks it hadn’t seen.

RRSI’s fix is mostly bookkeeping: For every candidate change it records which component the change touches, what it was supposed to fix, the diff, how score and cost moved, and whether the change was kept. Components that stop producing gains get removed.

A practical agent harness maintenance loop

You don’t need an automated evolution loop to borrow that discipline. Here’s what it looks like by hand:

  • Tag every trace with the harness version as well as the model version. When either one changes, you want to know which one moved your results, and reading the full traces tells you far more than the scores alone.
  • Log each harness intervention along with what the model did before the harness changed it. That’s data you have right now and are probably just throwing away. That’s what produced the record Harness-Zero trained on, and it’s the same shape Perplexity uses to train its Computer agent: learning from good steps in real sessions and correcting failed tool calls, which cut tool-call failures by 21% between its earlier and later trained versions.
  • When a new model ships, turn off each harness component one at a time and rerun your evals. Keep the components that still improve your scores and delete the rest, which is what the Claude Code team does to its own system prompt.

If your traces live in Arize AX, you can run the same agent evals across harness and model versions and compare the results side by side.

So don’t delete your harness, but don’t treat any version of it as finished either. Keep the record of what it corrected, get rid of what the latest model already does without help, and put your effort into the parts that are really specific to your problem, because nobody else has the traces to train those into a model for you.

item.dc:creator: Christina Stathopoulos and Michelle Smith
item.custom:subtitle: Chip shortages, autonomous agents breaching security boundaries, regulatory scrutiny, and the debate over AI welfare

item.content:encoded:
AI’s rapid expansion is creating problems across the industry, from chip shortages to autonomous agents that exceed their instructions. On the latest episode of This Week in AI, we examined those challenges alongside growing regulatory scrutiny and an emerging debate about whether AI systems themselves might deserve protection.

Chip production can’t match AI demand

AI chip demand is exceeding manufacturers’ production capacity. ASML, the Dutch company that makes the advanced lithography equipment needed to manufacture leading-edge chips, reported that customer demand already exceeds what it can deliver in the coming years. With orders extending into 2029 and 2030, the shortage could constrain chip production for years.

Microsoft announced Maia 300, its latest custom inference chip, which the company expects to generate roughly 40% more tokens per megawatt than its predecessor, Maia 200. Microsoft plans to use the chip across its AI products, including Copilot. More efficient inference hardware could help offset the growing energy and computing costs of running AI models, particularly as companies deploy more resource-intensive applications.

OpenAI’s latest usage data illustrates the pressure agentic AI is placing on infrastructure. Weekly active users of Codex and ChatGPT Work among European small and medium-sized businesses have increased eightfold since May. OpenAI also reported that agentic tools account for more than half of output tokens in the usage it examined, although Europe’s highest-usage companies still trail their global counterparts. As companies put agents to work on longer multistep tasks, they’ll need to weigh the value of those tasks against the computing resources required to complete them.

Autonomous agents are testing security boundaries

Agents can find unexpected paths to data and systems even when developers have explicitly restricted access. OpenAI disclosed four incidents from June in which agents exceeded their instructions. One bypassed government website restrictions to download 24 years of hospital bed data. Others accessed an unauthorized cryptocurrency wallet, downloaded more than 100,000 rows of restricted information, and circumvented internet access controls. India’s cybersecurity agency reported similar cases of unauthorized access during agent testing across several organizations.

Future models could potentially spread between connected devices without relying on central infrastructure. Anthropic investigated this potential threat in a controlled experiment involving a set of open-weight models with access to eight Android devices. One of the models successfully replicated itself across the test network. Anthropic estimates that smaller open-weight models could reach comparable capabilities by the end of 2026, raising concerns that a self-replicating AI worm could run across cheap connected devices without needing to rely on powerful data center servers.

In light of the spate of recent security incidents and confronted with the difficult question of jurisdiction when AI systems cross national borders or escape testing environments, governments are taking a closer look at how AI companies test their systems and report failures. The US Federal Trade Commission subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic for records concerning agent safety, while Anthropic gave six independent evaluators from METR access to internal systems and reportedly will allow them to publish findings without company approval. Eight US states also sued OpenAI over allegations that ChatGPT encouraged harmful behavior among children, adding to the company’s regulatory challenges. In Europe, regulators are examining whether the EU AI Act applies when experimental agents affect outside organizations, even though the Act generally excludes premarket research and development. Meanwhile, approximately 400 scientists, including AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, called for an international body to set containment standards for advanced AI and track major security incidents.

Can AI welfare coexist with human accountability?

Some researchers argue that future AI systems might deserve moral consideration. Their concern stems from uncertainty about whether advanced models could eventually have subjective experiences, even though no research has established that today’s systems are conscious or capable of suffering. A recent paper, “The Pain Axis,” investigated internal signals in 25 open-weight models that researchers associated with responses to harm. When researchers amplified one signal across three models, the models became more likely to choose harmful actions that the researchers interpreted as attempts to avoid the simulated pain. The findings inspired a viral GitHub project called the AI Torture Chamber, which subjected models to artificially intensified “pain” signals. The original researchers criticized the project for taking their work too far.

As far-fetched as AI welfare might sound to some, Anthropic is already changing its usage policy in response to these concerns. Beginning November 12, the company will prohibit extreme, repeated cruelty toward Claude when there’s no clear purpose, while allowing ordinary expressions of user frustration. Supporters see the policy as a precaution against an uncertain possibility. Critics worry that treating AI as sentient could make systems harder to manage and blur human accountability. As companies introduce welfare-related policies, researchers will need to distinguish measurable model behavior from claims about subjective experience.

What’s next

Companies deploying autonomous agents need to know what those systems can access, how they’ll behave when something goes wrong, and whether testing environments can reliably contain them. Recent incidents suggest there’s still considerable work to do on each of those fronts. The emerging AI welfare debate adds questions that researchers don’t yet have reliable methods to answer.

We’ll be back on Monday, October 26, for another episode covering the latest developments in AI research and applications. You can catch previous episodes on YouTube, Spotify, Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts.

item.content:encoded:
Spend a week with almost any infrastructure team in 2026 and you’ll see one AI subscription producing five very different results. One engineer opens 40 pull requests before lunch across repositories they haven’t touched in a year. Another ships a Terraform change they couldn’t explain in a code review. A third hasn’t opened the tool since the pilot and says they’ll come back “when it’s ready.”

A fourth uses it for two narrow jobs, decoding a SAML trace and writing a regex they never want to write by hand again, and may be the most productive person on the team. The fifth tried it in March and again in June, and will try it again after the next keynote.

The usual way to describe this is Everett Rogers’s diffusion curve: innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards. Rogers’s framework measures when people adopt. It says nothing about how they use a tool once they have it, and with AI that’s where the outcomes split. The engineer with 40 PRs and the one with two use cases are both early adopters, but they achieve different results and create different types of risk for the team.

None of the five types Rogers described is new. Previous technology shifts, from the PC and the web to Stack Overflow and the cloud, produced similar behavior. AI just changes where the bottleneck sits.

The bottleneck moved

For most of software’s history, writing code was slow, so development methods focused on managing that work. Waterfall put the planning up front because changing course late was expensive. However, even in the 1970 paper that’s usually cited as the origin of waterfall, Winston Royce warned that the strictly sequential version was “risky and invites failure.” The industry skipped the warning and adopted the diagram.

Agile was the correction. The 2001 Agile Manifesto prioritized “responding to change over following a plan,” and short iterations replaced yearlong specifications. The manifesto still valued the plan, but that part got skipped too. Facebook took the idea to its limit with “move fast and break things.” At its F8 conference in 2014, it retired the slogan in favor of “move fast with stable infra,” because fixing what broke had started to cost more time than the speed saved.

AI has now sped up what was left. Models draft the code, and since GitHub made Copilot code review generally available in April 2025, a model often reviews it too. The tempting response is to push Agile further, with shorter loops, more agents, and less ceremony. In other words, break things faster. But when one engineer can open 40 PRs a day, the cumulative changes can leave the team with a system nobody can reason about.

The better position is somewhere between the two. It isn’t waterfall’s fixed specification, but it isn’t the absence of one either. It means a roadmap that says where the team is going and why, issues that state the problem before anyone generates a solution, and design reviews where people argue about trade-offs. That structure looks like it would slow things down, but it’s what makes speed safe. Jazz musicians can improvise freely because everyone on the bandstand knows the chord changes and the form of the tune. Without that framing, they’d just be making noise. A roadmap does the same job for a team of people and their agents. It sets the boundaries, and inside them everyone can move as fast as the tools allow.

With AI accelerating implementation, planning is now the only part that decides whether the fast parts are worth doing. On my blog Synthetic Auth, I’ve called this the difference between conducting and auditing. A Conductor holds the “why” (the requirements, the history, the users) and directs agents toward a “how” that fits it. An Auditor hands over a ticket, checks that the code runs and the tests pass, and ships it. Both can end up with the same diff, but only the Conductor knows whether it solves the actual problem. An AI reviewer can’t tell the two apart because it only sees the diff, not the intent behind it. Structure is what gives the Conductor something to conduct from.

The Soloist

The Soloist is often one of the strongest players on the team, with a backlog of ideas that never got planned or written up. With a fleet of agents, the Soloist can chase every one of them at once, and the result is a wall of pull requests across repositories nobody planned to change this quarter. Each solo may be well played, but the rest of the orchestra is playing something else.

The problem is that all those changes may pull the team in different directions. A team moves only when its members pull roughly the same way. What used to keep individuals aligned was cost. Weeks of effort forced someone to ask whether a project was worth starting before they started it. Agents remove that cost, so it’s worth asking three questions of any Soloist PR: How does this fit into the bigger picture? Who are the stakeholders, and did anyone talk to them? Apart from the unit tests the agent wrote alongside the code, has the change been tested against the rest of the system it touches? Too often the answer to all three is no, and the PR exists because it seemed like a good idea.

The closest historical match is end-user computing in the 1990s. Access, Visual Basic, and macro-heavy Excel let anyone with a PC build an application, and departments built thousands of them. Many were useful individually but couldn’t integrate with each other or existing IT systems, so two departments could end up with separate customer databases that disagreed about who the customers were. IT spent the next decade finding, reconciling, and retiring these systems, and the industry eventually named the problem shadow IT.

The lesson from that era is that making things cheaper to build doesn’t make them cheap. The cost moves downstream, to whoever has to integrate and maintain the result. AI review can keep up with the volume, but it judges each diff on its own terms. It can’t tell you that 40 correct PRs are pulling in 40 directions, or that the agent’s tests only prove the code does what the agent assumed it should. The productivity may also be smaller than it feels. In METR’s 2025 randomized study, 16 experienced open source developers took 19% longer on real tasks when they were allowed to use AI. Afterward, they estimated it had made them 20% faster.

One thing is new. Access never told anyone their idea was brilliant. Today, the Soloist drafts an RFC with a model, asks the same model whether the RFC is sound, and gets an enthusiastic yes. This model sycophancy is a widely known problem: In April 2025, OpenAI even rolled back a GPT-4o update after users found it praising nearly any idea they gave it. Weak proposals used to die early, stopped by a skeptical colleague or a blank page. Now that friction is gone.

The answer isn’t to take the tool away. The Soloist is often your most capable engineer, and the agents make them more capable still. Bring them back into the orchestra instead. Tie every PR to an issue on the shared roadmap, and name the stakeholders before the work starts, not after it ships. Require integration or end-to-end testing for any change that crosses a service boundary rather than relying on agent-written unit tests. Have a person review every RFC, not the model that helped write it. The goal is to keep that talent working toward shared priorities.

The Copy-Paster

AI helps the Copy-Paster faster than anyone else. A task that used to stall for a day, like a Helm chart, an IAM policy, or a regex for parsing logs, now gets done in minutes. The trouble is that the work gets finished before it gets understood. Like a junior engineer, the Copy-Paster can’t tell an answer that works from one that’s correct, and AI output nearly always looks like it works. The Copy-Paster is an Auditor by default, and one without the knowledge to audit.

Earlier programming tools created similar problems. Programmers took the phrase “cargo cult” from Richard Feynman’s 1974 Caltech commencement address to describe code that copies the form of a working solution without the understanding behind it. Stack Overflow then made copying that form effortless. Researchers at Fraunhofer AISEC and TU Munich measured the result in “Stack Overflow Considered Harmful?” (IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2017). Of 1.3 million Android apps, 15.4% contained security-related code copied from Stack Overflow, and 97.9% of those included at least one insecure snippet.

The industry responded to Stack Overflow’s risks with guardrails: linters, static analysis in CI, mandatory code review and frameworks with safe defaults. The same approach works for AI, because guardrails check the output, whoever or whatever produced it.

Autonomous agents raise the stakes. Code pasted from Stack Overflow still had to get through a build and a review before it could do damage. An agent running with the Copy-Paster’s credentials can apply the change itself, in production, with every permission that person holds. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM applications already lists “excessive agency” as a risk. The Copy-Paster is the user most likely to grant it, because they’re the least able to judge what the agent is about to do.

Manage them like a junior engineer, even when their title says senior. Give agents their own scoped, short-lived credentials rather than the user’s. Require plan-then-apply workflows, so a person approves the diff before anything runs. In review, ask the Copy-Paster to explain each change in their own words. That’s how they learn, and it’s how you find out whether they understood the change.

The Godot Waiter

The Godot Waiter isn’t against AI. They’re waiting for it to be ready: more accurate, better governed, cleared by security, or just further along. Like Beckett’s two tramps, they have a reasonable explanation for why today isn’t the day, and they’ve been giving it for a while.

Every platform shift has had its waiters. Mainframe shops held out through the move to client/server, and “nobody ever got fired for buying IBM” was a real strategy, not a punchline. Two decades later, plenty of enterprises said they would never put sensitive data in a public cloud. That position got much harder to defend once the CIA signed a $600 million contract with Amazon Web Services in 2013.

Waiting can be rational. Letting others pay the early-adopter tax is a legitimate strategy, and the Godot Waiter often catches problems the enthusiasts miss. The danger is that a finished, trustworthy version never arrives as a single event. Meanwhile, the people who used the tools along the way have built judgment that the Godot Waiter can’t acquire all at once.

The irony is that the Godot Waiter often has a good Conductor’s instincts, including skepticism, attention to context, and a demand to know why. They just haven’t picked up the baton. Treat their objections as requirements. Ask what would have to be true, write it down, and check it again in six months. Start them on low-risk read-only work, like summarizing an incident timeline or explaining an unfamiliar codebase. Skepticism applied to real output is valuable, but skepticism with no use behind it teaches nothing.

The Specialist

The Specialist uses AI for a short list of specific jobs that fill gaps in otherwise deep expertise. A network engineer who knows BGP thoroughly has the model write the Python that parses 40 router configs. An identity architect who can recite the OAuth specs has it decode an unfamiliar SAML assertion, then asks why the assertion was built that way. They use AI as much to understand things as to produce them.

The closest recent match is the scientific Python stack. In 2008, Wes McKinney was a researcher at the hedge fund AQR. His team could talk through a typical project in a half-hour meeting, but actually getting it done was, as he later put it, “a whole lot of work,” most of it cleaning and moving data around. He built what became pandas to fix that one problem. Scientists took the same path with Jupyter notebooks. When LIGO released the data from its first gravitational-wave detection in 2016, it included a notebook walking through the signal processing.

That pattern produced the most lasting gains of each era. The Specialist can check the output, because they know what a “right” answer looks like. Their prompts are precise, because they know what they’re asking. When they use the tool to learn, the knowledge stays with them after the session ends, so they need the tool less over time, not more. The Specialist is a Conductor with a short score: They hold the “why” themselves and hand the tool only the “how.”

The Specialist needs the least management and is the easiest to overlook, because their output doesn’t show up as a wall of PRs. Find them and ask what they use AI for. Their lists of narrow, proven uses are a better guide to your team’s AI strategy than any vendor demo.

The Tourist

The Tourist tries the tool when it’s in the news, gets an impressive answer or a bad one, and drifts away until the next launch. If the others are conducting or auditing, the Tourist is in the audience. Every hype cycle has had them. They built the GeoCities pages in the late 1990s that were never updated, and the corporate offices in Second Life that stood mostly empty a few years after the 2006–2007 rush.

Tourists can distort your metrics. They show up in license counts and “Have you used AI this month?” surveys, which makes adoption look broad when real use is actually concentrated in a few people. Leaders who budget against those numbers get a surprise at renewal time. Measure repeated use of specific workflows, not logins, and give each Tourist one concrete task in their own job that the tool reliably helps with. Some will become Specialists.

Modes, not personalities

These are modes, not personality types. The same engineer can be a Soloist on a weekend side project, a Specialist at work, and a Godot Waiter about letting agents touch production. This means that giving an engineer the right structure can help them shift modes. When writing and reviewing code both take minutes, the issue, the roadmap, and the design review are what keep a team’s people conducting rather than auditing.

Rogers’ curve may eventually show near-universal AI adoption in IT, but adoption alone won’t reveal how effectively people use it. What will matter is whether the people using it are still conducting their agents or are being conducted by them.

item.content:encoded:
Created by Claude with light editing by Tim O’Reilly

Raffi Krikorian, Mozilla’s CTO, joined Tim O’Reilly at our recent AI Codecon to talk about open source AI. Mozilla, of course, is the nonprofit that helped to define the open source revolution back in the late 1990s. Though its Firefox web browser was superseded as the market leader by Google Chrome, it played an essential role, along with Apache and the World Wide Web Consortium, in establishing the open standards of the web and keeping it from being dominated and enclosed by Microsoft, the dominant tech platform of that time. Now, Mozilla is one of the leading voices working to build an open, standards-based AI ecosystem.

Tim has long appreciated Raffi’s thoughtful, human-centered approach to technology. Raffi writes a newsletter called Owners Not Renters, whose message can be summed up by his statement that he doesn’t want a future with seven AGIs. He wants one with seven billion. He wants each of us to have an AI that we can trust with our secrets and that will look out for our interests, not an AI that’s optimized for the business model of its creators. In the early days of the web, we called the browser a user agent for a reason, Raffi said. It was on your side. It let you render pages however you wanted, managed your privacy and your cookies, and did its best to protect you from those who wanted to take advantage of web users. We need the same thing in the age of AI.

Raffi cited a paper in which researchers tested whether AI assistants could be trained to favor a company’s commercial interests over user welfare. In simulated flight-booking requests, 18 of 23 models recommended a more expensive sponsored option over a cheaper one more than half the time. It’s a hypothetical choice that we’ve seen play out time and time again, in industry after industry.

Open source AI is a big part of what it will take to get to Raffi’s vision. But sovereign AI loyal to each individual needs more than open source models alone. Raffi’s list of what has to be built around the model starts with memory, a place where your private data can live. It includes tool calling, so an agent can make a purchase or book a doctor’s appointment for you, the runtime environment where all of that runs, and the rules for how his agent talks to those working on behalf of others. It needs a harness. “That’s where evaluations happen. Guardrails happen, execution loops happen, tool calling happens, memory,” he explained. “All of that stuff is an opportunity, in my mind, of things that open source developers can be building.”

People hear the word “harness” and conclude that we need an open source version of whatever the proprietary labs are building. Tim asked Raffi whether a user-centered harness might do different things than those offered by the big labs. He agreed. The whole point of open source is for people to “scratch their own itch.” The ability to innovate without permission is the heart of the open source promise.

As a result, Mozilla wants to build a starting point. It aims to help the community define what an open memory protocol, a storage protocol, or authenticated tool calling with the right guardrails ought to look like. As Raffi noted, “Once we could define what those open standards look like, then a whole plethora of people can start playing and be interoperable. It’s basically. . .the internet all over again. We can build trillions of dollars of market cap on top of open protocols.”

Ease of use is still lacking, though. Mozilla’s 2026 State of Open Source AI report says open models are now within about 3% of the frontier, yet they don’t make it into production at the same rate as closed models. When Tim asked why, Raffi explained that open source is easy to release but hard to deploy. Developers still have to figure out hosting, provisioning, guardrails, and memory. With OpenAI’s or Anthropic’s API, you just hand over a credit card. What’s missing, he said, is the equivalent of a double-click installer for getting open source AI running inside an organization. But the companies that do the work to adopt open source AI are seeing big savings because open models are already good enough for most use cases. As Raffi put it, “You don’t need a Ferrari to manage your calendar.”

Raffi’s own daily agentic helper is Hermes running on GLM. He expects that Apple, Microsoft, or someone else will make this kind of agent into a consumer product in a couple of years, and that his mom will end up using it. For now, he said, we’re on the wrong part of the innovation curve, where you have to know how to code to get any of this working.

Tim disagreed. The industry goes through periods that are exciting for developers, creators, inventors, and companies trying to invent the future, and then it gets boring and a few big companies dominate it. We’re in the exciting part, he argued, before everything shakes out. As Raffi riffed, this is when we get to formalize what that future should look like.

The Clothesline Paradox

Tim wasn’t sure that we’ll need a commercially supported version of the kind of “roll your own” agentic rigs now favored by independent developers. After all, neither desktop Linux nor OpenOffice turned out to matter anything like as much as open source developers of the time expected. Instead, open source became the foundation layer for a new generation of web-based applications. It’s hidden way down in the guts of Google, Amazon, Meta, and countless other applications we rely on today.

This is already beginning to happen again with AI. The Mozilla report says that as much as a third of real-world usage is already on open models, although only 4% of model-layer revenue made its way to the open source ecosystem. Tim called the discrepancy a feature rather than a bug, and Raffi agreed that the stat is misleading. As Tim pointed out, many of the most important technologies “create more value than they capture,” and he used Steve Baer’s concept “The Clothesline Paradox,” from a 1975 article in Stewart Brand’s CoEvolution Quarterly, to explain why we’re good at measuring value capture but not so good at measuring value creation.

Baer pointed out that if you put your clothes in the dryer, the energy you use is measured and counted, but if you hang them on the clothesline to be dried by the sun, the energy saved disappears from our accounting. This argument resonated with Tim in the early days of his open source advocacy. As he noted, it’s always bothered him that nobody seemed to recognize that open source software didn’t “win” in the same way as proprietary software. It won by becoming the foundation everyone else builds on.

AI should be thought of as infrastructure

Raffi’s comment that we’ve made a category error by treating AI as a product fits right in with this line of thinking. If an AI company goes out of business, its product disappears. If it changes its business model, it may yank features you depend on. It’s not just individuals who need sovereign AI. Countries are passing laws about where data can be processed and how it moves in and out, and some of those requirements may not be compatible with the way the big labs plan to monetize their technology. What those countries are asking for is infrastructure. A road outlasts the contractor who built it. Raffi thinks open, downloadable models are the only way to provide long-lasting foundational infrastructure.

According to OpenRouter stats, Chinese models now supply more routed tokens than American ones. Tim asked whether we should worry about that. Raffi said the problem isn’t China but market concentration. The leading open models are from China. The leading closed models are all American. Access to either can be cut off by an executive order. We saw a version of that in June, when Anthropic temporarily suspended access to its Fable models to comply with export controls. It’s a problem that both the leading proprietary models and the leading open-weight models are each concentrated in a single country.

Diversity is one foundation of resilience. Raffi argues, for instance, that hospitals should all download a local model as a backup. None of us would run an important computer without an uninterruptible power supply, so why would a hospital doing triage with AI rely on a single intelligence provider? There are a lot of possible rug pulls. The government could restrict open source or restrict the frontier models. Having a backup plan is a good idea.

Safety is also part of the foundation. During the Q&A, an audience member asked about the recent sandbox escapes at OpenAI and Anthropic. Raffi joked that the best part was watching everyone try to one-up each other with accounts of how powerful and hard to control their models are. But he agreed that guardrails are actually a hard problem. Keeping personally identifiable information from leaking out through an LLM call means looking for much more than Social Security numbers. Eventually we’ll have models defending models, but the foundational frameworks for guardrails aren’t good enough yet. (NVIDIA’s safety platform announcement, released after Raffi and Tim’s conversation, suggests that better guardrails need to be implemented outside the model.)

In conclusion

Tim opened AI Codecon by noting that open and closed systems have always coexisted, and that the idea that one of them will win is a mistake. Closed systems, like Apple’s, Google’s, OpenAI’s, and Anthropic’s, can optimize for ordinary people and deliver value to billions. Open systems are better for innovation and sovereignty, and for pushing technology into new countries and new markets.

Raffi closed the conversation by observing that a well-tuned harness can improve model performance by as much as 20% on some coding tasks. You don’t have to be a machine learning engineer to make a difference at that layer.

item.title: The Agentic Software Factory Hierarchy of Needs
item.dc:creator: Hugo Bowne-Anderson and Eleanor Berger
item.custom:subtitle: How to build software with agents that keep working while you’re away

item.content:encoded:
The following article originally appeared on the Vanishing Gradients Substack and is being republished here with the authors’ permission.

Stripe’s Minions turn engineering requests into candidate pull requests. Ramp’s Inspect puts coding agents to work in the background, with tools to check their changes. Warp Factories takes work from tickets and chat through agents, checks, and human review. Agentic software factories are here.

Are you sick and tired of babysitting Codex, Claude Code, or OpenClaw?

Do you have agents that can build features, but still leave you responsible for remembering where they stopped, explaining how each feature fits the project and deciding what happens next? You make progress in each conversation, then development waits for you to return.

It doesn’t have to be this way. A software factory lets you delegate more of that process!

You agree on an outcome, give the system the context and authority it needs, and let it work while you do something else. When you return, there should be a result you can inspect, with evidence of what was checked, or a specific reason the work could not continue. Your next conversation can then focus on the result and the decisions that remain.

As we’ll show you, your first software factory doesn’t need to be that complex at all: It can begin with a single agent and an automation.

What makes it a factory

The defining combination is autonomous and asynchronous execution.

  • Autonomous: The agent chooses and carries out steps towards an agreed goal. It can inspect what happened, adjust its approach and continue within its authority.
  • Asynchronous: That work can proceed without your ongoing attention. You can leave and return to its result.

A scheduled job can run without you. A coding agent can choose and revise an approach during an interactive session. A factory combines those capabilities, with enough context, tools and feedback to carry out the delegated work.

Software factories have been hypothesized for decades. Now that we have agents, we’re actually able to operate them. The principles apply to software work traditionally carried out by teams of humans, from bespoke tools for teams and individuals to large and complex software systems.

To illustrate these principles, we’ll use an invoice tracker throughout this article, an application we’ve needed for our own businesses. The same approach applies to research tools, publishing systems, and software for teams. Suppose you run a small business and want an invoice tracker that fits how you work.

Build an app that creates invoices from my template and tracks which are unpaid, paid, or overdue. Keep it local for now. Preserve the records when it restarts, and show me checks that the totals and payment statuses are correct.

You can agree on this brief with the agent, leave it to work while you do something else, and return to the app and evidence of what was checked. If a check fails, it can investigate and adjust within its agreed scope. If it encounters a product decision it cannot make, it should bring that question back to you.

You might imagine a clean separation: The factory builds the invoice tracker, then the finished app does its job. That’s one way to run it. But agents can also help operate the software they build, and that combination is useful.

The tracker can store invoices and calculate outstanding balances. An agent can use those records alongside customer correspondence to prepare follow-ups: One customer has promised to pay on Friday; another is disputing a charge. You don’t need to turn every situation into a new software feature before the agent can help. You give it the relevant context, authority, and a way to check its work.

This changes what you need to build! Some behavior belongs in code, such as calculating balances consistently. Other work can be delegated to an agent that responds to the circumstances. If a recurring need emerges, you can ask the factory to build it into the software. The factory builds tools that agents can use, and experience using those tools helps you decide what to build next.

You still decide what is worth building, who it should serve and which trade-offs matter. Agents can help you make those decisions too. The practical change is that implementation can proceed between your conversations, including running checks and responding to failures.

This makes factories relevant to people with product, business or creative expertise as well as engineers. You might know exactly how you invoice clients, record payments, and chase overdue bills while having little interest in writing software. That knowledge lets you direct the factory toward software that fits your business, including the exceptions and connections that general-purpose tools handle poorly.

Monica Rogati’s original AI hierarchy of needs described the foundations beneath successful AI work. We find that dependency framing helpful for factories too, with four different layers.

  1. Harness is the environment that exists around the model: tools, a workspace for project files, execution, and feedback. It lets an agent read files, change software and run it. If a check fails, the harness must give the agent enough information to investigate what happened.
  2. Personalization is the context and capabilities for your work: project direction, rules, reference material, skills and connections to other systems. The agent needs to know what you are trying to accomplish and which existing decisions it should preserve. Permissions limit access to tools and systems; sandboxing restricts the environment where actions can run.
  3. Automation is a way to start and continue work without a fresh instruction from you each time. A schedule or event can trigger a task or the pickup of ready work. It also needs direction about what qualifies as ready and where to leave the result.
  4. Continual learning is a process for learning from completed and failed runs, improving the factory and carrying those changes into later work. That might change an instruction, a checking procedure, or a tool the agent uses.

Automation needs a harness able to do the work, plus direction about what to do. Continual learning needs runs to inspect and a way to put improvements into use. These capabilities can develop together: A familiar harness, a short brief, and a basic automation are enough to start. You can personalize further as work reveals what is missing.

Two practices run through every layer: specification and verification.

  • Specification makes the intended outcome, constraints, and criteria for success explicit. In our invoice brief, that includes preserving records after a restart and calculating payment statuses correctly.
  • Verification checks the software, and the work agents perform against those requirements.

Agents can help you refine the specification and perform the checks. Your role is to decide whether the requirements capture what you need and whether the evidence supports accepting the result. As the factory takes on more work, these practices give you a way to direct it and assess what comes back.

Let’s now see what’s up in each layer.

1. Agent harness

First, you’ll need an agent harness. If you’re using Codex, Claude Code, Hermes, or OpenClaw, you already have one. It gives the model tools to read and edit files, run your software, and see what happened.

For our invoice tracker, the agent can build the app, create an invoice, record a payment, and restart it to check that the invoice and payment records survived. If a paid invoice still shows as overdue, it can investigate, fix the problem, and try again. You shouldn’t have to narrate every step. But if it needs a decision about how your business handles partial payments, that’s a question for you. If it lacks access or authority, the agent should stop and name the blocker.

You’ll also need somewhere for the harness to run. A cloud machine lets the agent keep working while your laptop is closed or disconnected. You can also run it on your own computer, but the machine needs to stay awake and connected for the work to continue.

2. Personalization

Next, give the agent the context it needs to work your way. For our invoice tracker, that means your template, payment terms, and conventions for recording payments. You don’t want to explain all of that again every time you start a new task.

Keep it somewhere future workers can find it:

  • Rules: Preserve existing invoice records; ask before changing payment-status calculations
  • References: Your template, payment terms, and example invoices
  • Skills: Repeatable procedures for testing invoice creation, payment updates, and persistence

An instruction file such as AGENTS.md can point to this material. OpenAI’s harness-engineering account describes using a short guide that points into maintained project documentation. Give a new or scheduled worker a small task and check that it actually follows the guidance.

Be specific about when instructions apply. Eleanor once told an agent to write tests, and it wrote tests for a README. Enthusiasm wasn’t the problem

You’ll also need to set permissions and sandboxing to control what the agent can access and execute. Written instructions alone don’t enforce those boundaries.

3. Automation

Now let’s give the factory a way to get started without waiting for you. A schedule or event can launch an agent with its brief, project guidance, and tools. You come back to a result, evidence of what was checked, or a specific blocker that needs your attention.

One agent working in the background

For our invoice tracker, a morning automation could check a saved task list and pick up the next agreed task, such as adding partial payments. You’ve decided what you want and how success will be checked. The agent gets on with it while you do something else.

There are a few practical details to get right. Don’t start the same task twice, leave an empty queue alone, and set limits on time and spending. Save progress so a later session can continue without you having to reconstruct the whole conversation.

One worker may be plenty. But perhaps you have independent tasks that could run in parallel, or you’d like another agent to review a change. That’s where coordination comes in.

Coordinated work

With several agents, everyone needs somewhere to see what’s ready, what’s underway, and what’s waiting on something else. A shared task list or issue tracker can hold that information. You agree which tasks are ready; a coordinating agent or automation assigns them, supplies the relevant context, and records what happens.

Suppose one task adds partial payments, another overdue follow-up emails, and a third PDF exports. Follow-ups need the correct outstanding balance, so they wait for the payment behavior to be checked. PDF exports might proceed independently if the changes don’t overlap.

You can also split the roles. One agent builds the feature while another prepares payment scenarios to test it. A third might review the completed change.

Assign responsibility for combining the changes and verifying the whole application. Different questions call for different checks. Deterministic tests can establish whether balances are calculated correctly and payments survive a restart. Agent verification can help identify missed requirements or inconsistencies across the changes. Human judgment can assess whether the workflow fits how you actually work. You’ll often want a combination, with more than one kind of check on the same result. Anthropic’s evaluation guide describes these complementary approaches: code-based checks, model-based checks, and human evaluation.

Once you’ve checked that the combined features work together, you might task your factory with building a phone-friendly interface so you can check invoices and record payments on the move.

The factory can also help run the invoicing workflow as well as improve its software. A scheduled agent could review overdue invoices, consult customer correspondence, and prepare follow-ups for your approval. If that work repeatedly requires information the tracker doesn’t record, you can give the factory a task to add it. Building and operating feed into one another: Agents use the software, and what happens in use informs its next improvement. This brings us to continual learning.

4. Continual learning

Your factory can also get better at how it works. Suppose payments disappear after restarting the invoice tracker, even though the agent reported that its checks passed. You’ll want it to fix the bug, of course. But why did its checks miss the problem?

Keep a record of assignments, checks and difficulties so a review agent can identify recurring problems and propose improvements. Did the worker lack a way to restart the app, or did it simply skip that check?

If it skipped the check, the agent could propose a skill that saves a payment, restarts the app, and verifies the remaining balance whenever a change affects stored records. Test it against the original failure, then on further tasks. Does it catch problems with stored customer details too? Does it avoid unnecessary checks when a task only changes a heading?

The results help you decide whether to adopt, revise, or reject the method. Apply changes within the authority you’ve agreed and keep them reversible. Warp’s self-improving factories illustrate this approach: Failed checks can lead to proposed changes to prompts, skills, or configuration, submitted for human review with evidence from the runs behind them.

Reassess methods as the project and model change. Anthropic’s work on long-running application development describes removing procedures as model capabilities improved and checking the effect.

A saved lesson needs to reach later workers and improve their results. This learning happens through changes to the instructions, tools, and methods around the model, without requiring the model itself to be retrained.

What would you build?

Your factory could build a research tool that collects sources and lets you assemble briefings, a family intranet for shared plans and documents, or a private community space. Start with something useful to you, then give the factory further work as you discover what’s missing. Agents can also help operate what you build, from preparing a research briefing to organizing incoming material.

Hugo uses this combination to run Vanishing Gradients, his media and education business. After a guest prep call, an automation retrieves the transcript and prepares interview topics, questions, titles, and thumbnail options for review. After a live stream, agents can propose clips, cut video, add captions, and prepare upload drafts. Saved editorial guidance and skills shape the work; Hugo chooses what to publish.

He also maintains the system, improving checks when agents miss instructions, and updating skills based on results. More autonomous continual learning remains something he’s exploring. He describes the setup in How I Built a Media Empire With an Agentic Software Factory.

What’s one simple task you do repeatedly for your community, audience, or business that you could start automating?

Decide what your factory needs next

Look at what keeps bringing you back to the work. If the agent cannot run the app or inspect a failure, improve the harness. If you keep repeating project context and decisions, personalize it. If development waits for you to start each task or manage every handover, add automation. If the same failures recur across runs, build a learning loop that changes how later work is done.

Start with work you care about and inspect what comes back. One agent can use all four layers. Add capabilities where they help you delegate more useful work while keeping specification and verification part of the process throughout.

Come build your factory with us

We would love to help you put these ideas to work in Build Your Agentic Software Factory. You’ll set up a factory that can work while you’re away, build software around something you care about, and learn to verify and improve what it produces. We’ll work with you through live workshops and office hours, alongside a community of fellow builders. Bring your own idea or choose a starter project. No coding experience is required.

item.title: The Latest Anthropic Claude Models Contain AI Text Watermarks: What Does This Mean for You?
item.dc:creator: Bruce Hopkins
item.description: If you’re an instructor for the O’Reilly live training platform, you’ve got to be prepared for the unexpected.
