item.content:encoded:
In my previous article, I argued that agentic development needs enough specification to make correctness checkable. A quick prompt can get implementation started quickly, but someone still has to decide whether the result does what we wanted. I left a fairly practical question unanswered, though. Once the agent has written the code, how should we review it?

You can give an agent a clear task and get back a serious implementation with tests. The build passes and the code looks reasonable. Now somebody has to approve the pull request, and that person has roughly the same amount of time they had before code generation became cheap.

Reading every changed line is one way to approach this. But if each increase in generated code requires a similar increase in human inspection, review will keep limiting how many changes we can accept. We need a way to decide where that inspection is worth the effort.

My approach is to make evidence a condition of accepting agent-generated code. Agree on the intended behavior and the expected blast radius before implementation starts. Then use the evidence to check for drift and decide which parts of the code need direct inspection. So far, that may sound like test-driven development. But what happens when every test passes and the agent has added behavior nobody asked for?

A small diff can have a large blast radius

Let’s use a small fictional example. Suppose we are adding an approval step to a refund service. Refunds above €100 require approval from an authorized employee before the service sends the payment request. Exactly €100 does not require this additional approval. The existing rules about who can request a refund continue to apply.

An agent implements the approval step and adds tests. While updating the payment integration, it also adds retries after a timeout. That seems reasonable enough. Network calls fail, and retrying them is a familiar engineering practice.

But a timeout leaves us with another question. The provider may have issued the refund before its response was lost. Sending the request again could issue a second refund. Whether that can happen depends on how the provider handles repeated requests and how our code uses that behavior. The approval feature may be correct while the added retry introduces a separate problem. I can see a human review focusing only on the requested feature and easily missing the new decision about payment behavior.

By blast radius, I mean how far the effects of a mistake can spread. If the agent puts the retry in a shared payment client, it may affect every refund, including those below the approval threshold. The change now reaches beyond the feature we asked for. Counting the changed lines won’t tell us that.

Treat blast radius as a review criterion on its own. Establish which operations a change is allowed to affect, then check whether the implementation stays within that boundary. Also consider how hard a mistake would be to undo. Deploying the previous version won’t recover money that has already been refunded twice.

Look for drift in both directions

This is the kind of drift I want a review process to expose. We need to check that the requested behavior exists and examine additional behavior that could affect the system.

There is an established name for following these relationships in both directions: bidirectional traceability. NASA’s software engineering guidance describes tracing requirements through implementation and verification, including finding functionality that has no parent requirement. I think that the basic idea translates quite well to an ordinary pull request.

For each important requirement, we should be able to find the implementation and the checks that support it. Looking back from the implementation, we should be able to explain why a change to behavior belongs in this pull request. An extra private method will usually need little discussion. A retry that changes how money moves needs a reason we can review.

Of course, an unplanned addition isn’t automatically a mistake. The retry might be necessary. Implementation often reveals something the original specification missed. We can accept the new behavior once we understand its consequences and agree on how to check it. Until then, it remains an open decision.

An agent can help identify these relationships. Give it the agreed specification and the actual repository changes, and ask it to find behavior that is missing or unexplained. For the refund service, that should include the changed payment client even if the agent’s own summary only mentions the approval feature. Start with the changed files so that the summary doesn’t determine what gets examined. Follow those changes into their callers, too. A shared client can change the behavior of code that has not been edited.

The tests can share the same mistake

While this is a general direction for our attention in a review, the links themselves tell us very little about correctness. A method can reference the right requirement and still implement it incorrectly. A test can have exactly the name we hoped to see and check the wrong result.

Consider the threshold again. Suppose the agent reads “above €100” as “€100 and above.” It uses the same interpretation when writing the tests. The implementation requires approval for exactly €100, and the test expects that behavior. Everything passes because the code and the test agree.

Running that test in a separate CI environment will reproduce an agreement but it won’t discover that the expected result was wrong. We still need someone to check the meaning of the assertion against the agreed behavior. Spend some of the review time on these expected outcomes. For a requirement like this, agreeing on the boundary examples before implementation is quite manageable. A refund of €100 proceeds without the additional approval. One cent more must wait. The reviewer can then inspect whether the tests actually observe that difference. Have the test observe what the service sends to the payment provider. Checking that an approval request was created is insufficient if the service can also send the payment immediately. For refunds above the threshold, the test should check that the payment request cannot leave the service before approval. That checks the rule at the point where the refund is requested.

For an important rule, you can go a little further. Temporarily remove the approval check in a controlled test run and see whether the relevant test fails. If it stays green, it gives us very little protection. Google’s code review guidance asks reviewers to consider exactly this kind of question: Will the tests fail when the code is broken?

Use another agent to propose cases we forgot and examine whether the assertions match the requirement. Keep the actual checks available to the human reviewer, though. A different model can still produce the same miss-interpretation. There is some research backing up that caution. A 2026 study of LLM requirement-conformance judgments found models rejecting correct implementations and accepting faulty ones. The study used programming benchmarks, so it does not tell us how every review agent will behave in a production repository. It does give us a reason to look beyond a model’s confident explanation when deciding whether code meets a requirement.

Make the evidence easy to inspect

Require a short review record with each pull request. It should connect the intended behavior to the checks and expose decisions that remain open. For our hypothetical refund change, it could begin like this:

  • Agreed behavior: Refunds above €100 wait for authorized approval before payment. Exactly €100 does not need that additional approval.
  • Evidence: Boundary tests check when the payment request is sent. The review links to their assertions and the CI results for this revision.
  • Additional behavior: The payment client now retries after a timeout.
  • Blast radius: If the retry applies to the shared client, all refund requests may be affected. Review its existing callers.
  • Open question: The tests do not cover a provider completing the refund before the timeout. Safe retry behavior still needs to be established.

Start the review with this record. Check that the approval assertions express the agreed rule and that the results support it. Then inspect the retry path, where both the evidence and the intended scope are incomplete. Require a test covering the uncertain provider response or remove the retry from this change. The open question has become a concrete review decision. Link each claim to the checks that support it. “Tests passed” is too broad to help much. The reviewer needs to see which tests ran against the revision being approved. If the agent changes the implementation after that run, refresh the evidence.

Review changes to the checks

Compare the checks with the agreed baseline as well. Suppose an earlier acceptance test expected a €100 refund to proceed, but the agent updates it to expect an approval request. The new implementation and the new test now agree. Comparing both with the agreed requirement exposes the change in meaning. An agent does not have to be trying to hide anything for this to happen. Updating a test to match new behavior is part of everyday development. The reviewer needs to decide whether that new behavior was intended. Changes to acceptance criteria deserve the same attention for the same reason.

Sometimes the new behavior will be the right approach. Perhaps the business actually wants approval starting at €100. Fine, we can change the requirement. Record that decision and review its consequences before accepting the implementation. Quietly changing the spec to match the code leaves us with agreement and no explanation of how we got there.

Set review depth by blast radius

Match the depth of review to the potential impact and the strength of the evidence. A report can only expose the gaps it detects. Tests can pass even when the code relies on a wrong assumption. Require direct inspection of the payment path because a mistake can move money twice. Follow the affected calls even if some of them sit outside the diff.

For a routine change with limited effects and established checks, the reviewer can spend less time reconstructing the implementation. The justification is specific: The affected behavior is understood, and the checks address its likely failures. Where the blast radius is unclear, investigate it before approving changes. Occasionally inspect changes that the process treated as routine, too. If those reviews keep finding missing assumptions, improve the checks before relying on them to reduce inspection further. This gives the team a way to test its review policy against the code it is actually accepting.

Make evidence part of the development cycle

Here is the process I recommend. Before generation starts, a developer agrees on the behavior and its expected blast radius with whoever owns the requirement. The agent implements within that scope and prepares a short review record. CI runs the checks against the proposed revision. The reviewer examines the evidence and investigates deviations, with direct code inspection where the consequences justify it. Release through a controlled rollout, then use what happens in production to improve the checks and the specification.

Make the review record part of the definition of done. The developer submitting the change owns its accuracy, even when an agent writes it. The reviewer owns the acceptance decision. An important claim with inadequate evidence stays open. If the implementation affects more operations than agreed, resolve that change in scope before proceeding.

For the refund example, that means the approval feature can proceed once its checks support the agreed behavior and the reviewer has examined the relevant payment path. The added retry needs its own justification. It can be removed or reviewed as an explicit addition, with evidence that repeated requests will not issue duplicate refunds. This builds on familiar development practices. Acceptance examples clarify intent before coding. CI repeats the checks, and small releases limit exposure. The proposal joins those practices around the review decision so that evidence is available when the implementation arrives. It also keeps review effort reusable: Once the approval boundary is checked correctly, later changes can run the same test.

Keep the blast radius contained

Keep the approval feature separate from a redesign of the shared payment client unless the two need to change together. Separate pull requests help reviewers assess each decision, but containment also depends on the implementation. A one-line change in a shared client can still affect every caller.

Use the same discipline with your releases. Where the system supports it, expose the change to a limited group (A/B) and watch the affected behavior before expanding the rollout. For refunds, that still requires adequate checks before any real payment. Start with one service and make this the normal way changes reach review. Require the evidence, record the expected blast radius, and keep unexplained behavior open until someone resolves it. Reduce routine line-by-line inspection as the checks earn trust. Keep direct inspection where a mistake has serious consequences. That is a concrete way to accept more agent-generated code while keeping the effects of each change understandable and contained.

item.title: Generative AI in the Real World: Observability for AI with Charity Majors
item.dc:creator: Ben Lorica and Charity Majors
item.category: Generative AI in the Real World
item.description: AI makes it possible to generate code faster than teams can understand and support it. In this episode, Honeycomb cofounder and CTO Charity Majors joined Ben to discuss how that shift changes the work of building reliable software. Charity explained how observability helps teams connect changes with outcomes, why nondeterministic systems need “more rigor, not […]
item.content:encoded:
AI makes it possible to generate code faster than teams can understand and support it. In this episode, Honeycomb cofounder and CTO Charity Majors joined Ben to discuss how that shift changes the work of building reliable software. Charity explained how observability helps teams connect changes with outcomes, why nondeterministic systems need “more rigor, not less,” and how traces can show the decisions agents make along the way. Over their wide-ranging conversation, she and Ben also covered automatic instrumentation with OpenTelemetry, why we should think of ourselves as “owners on the loop,” the limits of AI in debugging and SRE, and broader industry concerns like the pressure AI hype places on engineering teams and why maintenance, not speed, builds “enduring value.”

About the Generative AI in the Real World podcast: In 2023, ChatGPT put AI on everyone’s agenda. In 2026, the challenge will be turning those agendas into reality. In Generative AI in the Real World, Ben Lorica interviews leaders who are building with AI. Learn from their experience to help put AI to work in your enterprise.

Check out other episodes of this podcast on the O’Reilly learning platform or follow us on YouTube, Spotify, Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Takeaways

00.59. “Observability is for unknown unknowns.” Monitoring is a way to set thresholds and alert on expected conditions. Observability supports open-ended investigation to answer questions you didn’t know to ask and “find things you didn’t expect.” When AI code generation became capable enough to change software work, observability best practices had to evolve, which is one reason why the second edition of Observability Engineering, which Charity coauthored with Liz Fong-Jones and George Miranda, more than doubled in size.

05.24. Cheap code shifts the work to understanding and support. AI can quickly produce implementation, tests, and documentation, but teams still need to understand what they built and agreed to support, and how their users are experiencing the product. As generating lines of code becomes “effectively free and instant,” validation, review, and operational support can constrain a team’s pace. Of course, Charity wryly noted, so can “every other part of the software development lifecycle.”

06.24. The people who take the credit for AI-assisted work should be able to explain it. AI-generated results (and the papers describing them) complicate authorship, expertise, and the academic training process, something that’s become a particular point of consternation for mathematicians of late. If someone is claiming a result they accomplished with the help of AI, they should be able to present it to peers, Charity and Ben agreed. When AI handles entry-level problems, professions may need new ways for junior practitioners to develop mastery, but Charity is skeptical we’ll run out of problems to solve:

In the same way that I’ve made peace with the idea that cars are faster than I can walk or run, I have made peace with the fact that computers can compute better than I can. . . .That doesn’t mean that there’s no value in the practice, or the discipline, or the learning, or the rigor. It just means that this is one of the things that humans are no longer the best at. But there are a lot of things that we are the best at, and being the best at something isn’t all of what makes it worth doing.

15.56 Nondeterministic systems require “more rigor, not less.” As Charity noted, “The future of software is both determinism and nondeterminism. It really is about using these superpowers that we’ve been given to build those feedback loops. And observability is really the feedback loop of feedback loops.” It’s what connects actions with outcomes and helps teams learn what happened after they make a change. Her analogy:

It’s like we’ve all been riding lawnmowers and just kind of putt-putt, putt-putt, putt-putt along down the road. And now, all of a sudden, our lawnmower has a Ferrari motor in it, and we’re like, “Vroom!” Now we can vroom into the ditch. We can run into a wall. And we have to build structure. We have to build rigor into our system if we want to run down the middle of the street.

18.53 People need to own the loop, and understand the decisions the agents are making. If you need to add observability to your agents, Charity recommends starting with autoinstrumentation with OpenTelemetry and traces that capture agents’ decisions and steps through a task. As for your role, it goes beyond staying “in” the loop. Charity prefers the term “owner on the loop” because it emphasizes the active understanding and control required to manage these systems. AI can amplify experienced debugging and SRE teams, especially when people direct work during rare, high-stakes incidents. Agents have little training data for those situations and can make an incident harder to diagnose. These tools are “not magic,” Charity pointed out. AI “is not a replacement for expertise, but it can be a really powerful adjutant. . .at your side.”

26.00 Different telemetry needs different strategies. Charity distinguished the abundant output from third-party infrastructure from the business-critical telemetry produced by a company’s own code.

There’s observability for infrastructure, which is mostly third-party code. . . .It’s code you didn’t write, but you have to operate it. You can’t change it, but it’s just outputting a lot of logs and metrics into your database logs and your ETLs, or CloudWatch, and all this third-party code is just emitting a lot of stuff. . . .That stuff you should just put someplace that is cheap commodity storage. . . .It shouldn’t be super expensive, just that it’s there when you need it.

Then there are your crown jewels: your code, the code that makes you the company. . . .You should instrument in such a way that preserves as many of the relationships between the data points as possible: arbitrarily wide structured-data blobs, structured logs, and/or traces with lots of spans. Because the most valuable part of your data is the relationships. . . .You don’t want to spread it out into hundreds or thousands of individual metrics or log lines. You want to keep it together so that you can correlate: when this happened, that happened; or when this happened, that was true; or when this happened, it was part of this long event. . . .This is the most important data you have. And for that, it should go someplace. . .that preserves those relationships and opens it up for explorability by you or your agents.

item.custom:subtitle: Quality now depends on the constraints you set around your agents

item.content:encoded:
The following article originally appeared on Addy Osmani’s Elevate blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission.

For much of human history, we’ve evaluated code quality via code review: Someone reads what you wrote and makes sure it’s clean, thoughtful, fast, understandable, and tests well. For agents, that approach doesn’t scale well; there’s just too much code for anyone to read. As a result, more and more of our quality checks have to happen in the harness, environment, and operating system around the agent. I still read and review code, but am very intentional about where I am comfortable with constraints as the check.

Software quality now depends on the constraints you set around your agents.

Constraints define what the system is allowed to do by throwing tests and deterministic constraints at an agent’s proposals. It’s by setting and maintaining these constraints that we build loops that reliably deliver high-quality production software, even when agents are creating hundreds of thousands or millions of changes every single day.

We call these constraints quality gates, and they take many forms. They include conventional unit tests, property tests, and acceptance tests. They include mutation testing, where we generate variations of code, run it against the same tests, and make sure that people aren’t sneaking bugs in that we’re missing. They’re metrics around code quality, such as cyclomatic complexity and line length, that help keep things readable. Constraints also play an important role in what proposals the system will accept and apply as code changes. By the time a change proposal moves from the interpreter running the agent to the agent controller and out to production, we’ve done enough checks on it to be confident that it’s safe to ship and the impact of its change is well within the scope of the agent.

An agent can propose anything. Your constraints decide whether a proposal is safe enough, correct, scoped, and useful, for you and your team to ship.

This model offers a lot but also leaves out many pieces, and those omissions are worth thinking about today. One issue is autonomy; agents might apply their intentions well but may fail when there’s missing information or when what they try to do is ambiguous. That applies both to the task itself and to how it’s parameterized by the harness, environment, and other components. Many of the reasons that humans fail to ship great code are shared with what agents might do: brittle environments that don’t hold up under script-driven stress, nondeterministic builds, missing permissions, and weak tests. This motivates a better environment that gives agents trustworthy feedback, allows for low-damage failure modes, and makes it easier to progressively build up success.

The environment we’re after is one where an agent can do real work, get feedback it can trust, and fail without doing much damage.

The other important issue is trust. We can’t credulously hand off intent to something even as smart and robust as a modern agent without checking for correctness. We start with trust, but it has to be hard-earned.

Some constraints shape work before it begins. Others give feedback while the agent is working. Others decide whether its output can cross the production boundary at all.

There are a bunch of ways to model how we put a verification structure around a system.

In my experience it helps to have a broader, but intentionally chosen, set of checks for your constraints instead of relying solely on unit tests. The idea is that each check has a distinct responsibility, and that can range from type safety and performance to late-stage security scanning. Folks can define their own constraints too, including architecture rules that linting tools like ESLint can enforce. Many of these tools have built-in hooks that can be used to pull in agents, or humans, when things break.

For now, much of the difference between useful agent output and slop still comes down to the skill of the team operating the loop.

AI gives us high-volume code generation and velocity, but this can also mean it gets harder for humans to review every single change. You have to instead be intentional with where their attention is going. If you put a human check into a system that otherwise moves at machine speed, don’t be surprised if that impacts productivity. Human attention is scarce and valuable, so we should proactively direct it to those most nuanced problems that require our judgment. Downstream humans should only be pulled in when the automated guardrails for constraints break.

Human “code review” in the future is going to look very different.

Correctness is one important dimension, but you may care about others as well, like maintainability, performance, security, efficiency, and comprehensibility. Just as correctness decomposes into many signal types, so too does the rest of quality. And while it matters how many constraints we have in place, it matters more whether they’re challenging enough to meet our bar for quality and production readiness.

Software quality isn’t a single metric. Think of it as a collection of signals of varying importance to you and your team.

Back-pressure can be implemented through many tools: compilers rejecting invalid code, tests failing, security policies blocking bad practices, CI declining to deploy. Ideally it exists throughout the loop, not as a single review at the very end of all the work.

Constraints and back-pressure let agents catch bad work before it’s a problem.

What happens if we can’t apply the constraint because the volume of changes is higher than our tools can consume? We end up building a queue and relying on a verification system that moves at human speed. To scale, we want to push as much as we can into the verification loop throughout and not wait until the end. If we can scale within our automated checks, we can increase the speed and throughput of our entire delivery system. If we run out of room in the verification loop, we need to do one of several things. First, we can scale our verification system and create more capacity to constrain and push back on changes that come in. Second, we can reduce the rate at which agents generate new changes so that verification can catch up to the volume of work. Third, we can lower our quality bar so that verification doesn’t push back as hard as it otherwise might. From a scaling perspective, we need to be ready to do all of these things. At the same time, we should not stop short of realizing that we could actually get more done by unconstraining in some directions. Maybe we can increase the speed of agent-generated changes by providing swarms of agent developers or automated software factories to create changes without waiting for us to review each of them.

And in some places we might want to give them more freedom as long as we keep tighter constraints in others. By providing tighter constraints where we care the most, we can maximize our throughput without sacrificing quality. Throughout these decisions there are many options. Most obviously, we have to trade between different dimensions of quality. As we’ve emphasized, security is very important, but we’ve also had to trade between delivering security and delivering a product on time. There is a spectrum from innovation-focused at one end to quality-focused at the other. Somewhere along the way, we have to make choices about where we want to be on that spectrum.

We want to send clear feedback from the environment and the system back to our agents or teams, so that people can focus on the more subjective concerns of taste, intent, and architecture. If we can help humans stay inside the safe range of constraints, we can avoid the need for them to work hard trying to figure out where things went wrong.

Software quality includes more than just correctness. Software quality also means maintainability, good performance, security, efficiency, and being easy to understand. All the constraints that help us meet these standards and keep our production flowing create back-pressure in our delivery pipeline.

We need to make deliberate decisions about where to apply strong constraints and where to remove or relax them. Apply strong constraints where they’re serving both of these goals. Don’t support them if they’re not serving one or both. Be ready to raise or lower standards as the case may require. And remember these constraints at different points in the software system are what make software quality enforceable.

We should apply strong constraints where they’ll serve this dual purpose best and consider removing or relaxing constraints that aren’t serving either purpose well. We should also be ready to shift quality bars up or down as needed. In effect, these constraints at various points in our software system are what give quality its teeth. In many cases, we can create more back-pressure and more constraints by deploying new tools or strengthening tools that are already in place. All of these things can be used to push back on most change requests. We want to build them throughout the pipeline. We don’t want to wait until the end of the pipeline when our CI system will simply tell us that we’re not allowed to deploy without fixing problems. We want to use these signals as early as we possibly can, through every possible pathway. The ultimate constraint in this system is the one we place on ourselves to stand behind the decisions and actions we’ve taken to build the system and to operate it. But like all other constraints, we need to make thoughtful trade-offs about how much we want our own judgment to restrain, to back-pressure, and to act as a final check.

Quality is in the constraints that we place around our agents. So as you’re thinking about quality for your own apps, take this problem statement and come up with your own constraint-driven plan.

item.content:encoded:
I use AI for writing all the time. But not because it’s good at writing.

In fact, just the opposite is true. AI is so reliably bad at writing that I’ve actually taken advantage of that, and made its bad writing an integral part of my writing process.

I’ve written a lot of books and articles over the years, and while I used to start with an outline, I don’t anymore. These days I do a lot of brain dumping and brainstorming and talking out loud to an AI, working out what I think about something. I accumulate a lot of notes and ideas, and run a lot of experiments, and at some point, if I’m lucky, I decide there might be an article somewhere in all of that.

Then I ask the AI to take everything I’ve given it and write a draft.

And that AI-generated draft is universally terrible. Like, some of the worst writing you can imagine.

Which is exactly what I want.

Instead of an outline, I get an entire “article” or “chapter” (or, at least, a weird facsimile of one), with paragraphs that express complete thoughts that I gave the AI. Granted, those paragraphs are full of obvious AI tics, like how it uses em dashes to squish two unrelated sentences together, or weird staccato sentences one after another, or these insufferable parades of sentence fragments. Maybe the worst tic is that half of the paragraphs AI generates have an extra sentence that doesn’t actually say anything, but just delivers a forced conclusion with fake “punchiness.” I guess maybe AIs were trained on a lot of bad writing? Well, whatever, it works for me.

The reason I love that type of obviously bad AI writing is because when I’m looking at one of its paragraphs, it’s immediately obvious that an AI wrote it. I’ve been thinking of it as a kind of an improved “lorem ipsum” that lets me see how my article will look, while still serving as a functional placeholder. That lets me use it the way I would use an outline: I can move parts of the article around, make sure it flows correctly, and then replace ALL of the bad AI writing with (hopefully) decent human writing, just like I used to do with bullets in my old outlines.

One weird side-effect of writing this way is that it’s made me very sensitive to the different kinds of AI tics and tells. And I think the weirdest and most frustrating one is “Yoda-speak,” where the AI literally talks like Yoda. It’s weird, kind of hilarious, annoying, and pervasive, but most of all, it’s fascinating. Why does the AI keep talking like Yoda? What causes it? Can we do anything about it? (Do we even want to? It certainly makes it easy to identify AI-generated text, and also, it’s often unintentionally hilarious.)

I’ve got a theory about why this happens, and I ran an experiment that generated some evidence to support it. But first… what, exactly, is Yoda-speak?

Backwards, this bad writing is

I’ve been working on my latest book. It’s called Be the Model, and it teaches you how LLMs work by having you build interactive pages that let you literally do the job of a model to get an intuitive understanding of how they work. So I’ve been writing a lot, which means I’ve been confronted with a lot of Yoda-speak.

Here’s a great example from the chapter I’m currently working on (the “pond sentences” are a small training text), from a description of a page that you’ll build to learn how training works:

The eight pond sentences fill the left region, every word clickable.

That’s weird, right? Nobody talks like that.

To be perfectly fair, I’ll need you to suspend your disbelief a little. Yoda would probably say something more like, “The left region, filled by the eight pond sentences is. Clickable, every word must be.” But the AI-generated version is still very weird, and in a pattern that is recognizably Yoda-like.

That’s a pattern I’ve seen a lot. At one point I was looking through some AI-generated text, trying to figure out a particularly unintelligible sentence. When I asked Claude Opus for help, it came up with the term “Yoda-speak,” and I’ve since found that using that term is really useful when trying to get an AI to help decipher sentences like that.

The interesting thing is that AIs are perfectly capable of detecting and correcting Yoda-speak. You can try this yourself: start a new ChatGPT session, paste in that “pond” sentence, tell it: “An AI generated that sentence. That’s Yoda-speak.” I just tried that in an incognito window, and here’s the answer it just gave me:

Yep —that’s unmistakably Yoda-speak. A natural version would be:

“The eight pond sentences fill the left region, with every word being clickable.”

Or, more naturally for UI instructions:

“The left region contains the eight pond sentences, and every word is clickable.”

The original sounds like the AI took normal English, rearranged the syntax, and then forgot to put it back.

This particularly ugly sentence, from one of those AI-generated outlines of a later chapter that I haven’t started writing yet about the attention mechanism (the part of the LLM that understands context and relationships between words), is the example that made me want to write this article:

What’s left is to let the two heads’ work combine, so run the combined eight numbers through one more small table, eight in and eight out, square, called the output projection.

Ugh.

The problem with that sentence, and what made it hard to diagnose what was going on, is that when you first look at it you can basically understand what it’s saying (sort of?), and it’s hard to put your finger on exactly what’s wrong with it. It’s obviously terrible writing, but that’s not unique. AI is a universally awful writer.

What’s uniquely wrong with that sentence is its weird, comma-laden structure. Different parts of the sentence are split up into small comma-separated phrases, and AIs seem especially prone to using them to rearrange sentences, often at the expense of readability. That particular sentence is about running a combined set of eight numbers through one additional small 8×8 table. But the part of the sentence that should have described the table was in the second half of the sentence, and then you learn at the very end that the whole thing is called an output projection (but only after you’ve already been told to run numbers through it). Somehow the components of the sentence were arranged in a way that made it almost unintelligible.

One word at a time, it writes

An LLM is a next-word predictor. It works by taking your prompt, all of the context you’ve fed it, and everything it’s generated so far, generating the next word in its response, and then repeating the whole process for the next word, then the next one, and so on. It’s counterintuitive to think that AIs could possibly work that way, because these things can produce long, complex, and generally coherent and helpful responses. It seems very strange that they do all of that work one word at a time, without following a master plan for a response.

But that’s literally how the AI works. Once an LLM generates a word, it’s part of the response. It generally can’t go back and rearrange the first half of a sentence, even though it hasn’t finished generating it.

And that brings me back to that especially weird “eight in and eight out, square” barely intelligible sentence. Here’s what I think happened. The model generated the sentence up through “run the combined eight numbers through one more small table,” so those words were already baked into the response. Then it figured out that it had three more things it wanted to say about that table. But by that time it was too late to go back and put those details where they belonged, and apparently there was a shortage of periods that week, or possibly a surplus of commas (there’s no way to know for sure), so it just smashed each of those thoughts onto the end of an already awkward sentence.

I did some research to try to figure out if anyone has looked into this phenomenon before. The closest thing I found to an answer is a 2024 paper by Wilson Wu, John X. Morris, and Lionel Levine called “Do language models plan ahead for future tokens?” They were attempting to determine whether a model does real advance work for words it hasn’t written yet, or whether the information that pays off later is a byproduct of whatever was useful at the time.

The experiment that Wu et al. did was actually pretty clever. In normal training, when the model is being corrected for mispredicting a word several steps ahead, that correction reaches back and shapes what it computed at earlier positions. That way, the model learns to prepare information at an early word for the benefit of words further along, which is the “planning ahead” the paper is testing for. So they trained one model normally, and a second one with a modified process that cut that out: each position could only be trained to help predict the very next word. They kept next-word prediction but removed the training signal from words two or more steps ahead.

Then the researchers compared how well the two models predicted text: if the normally trained model did better, that would be evidence that preparing information in advance was actually helping. With ordinary language, the difference was fairly small for GPT-2, although it became larger as they tested bigger models.

So there’s evidence that a model can sometimes prepare information that will be useful later, which means my story about it only figuring things out as it goes is probably too simple. But anticipating is not revising. Whatever the model sees coming, it still can’t reach back and reorder the words it already committed to, and the words it already committed to are where the damage shows up.

Better, the second answer often is

I have a theory that the Yoda-speak phenomenon is closely related to something I see all the time (and I expect you do, too). Say you’re asking an AI for help with an email, and it gives you a draft of a sentence. Then, immediately after it gives you that sentence, it says something like this: “A better way to phrase that would be:” and gives you a second version. Sometimes there’s even a third option. And it almost always tells you it prefers the last one that it generated.

Coincidentally, I ran into a good example of that “here’s a better version” phenomenon when I asked ChatGPT to make the pond sentence more Yoda-like. I literally gave it the prompt make it more yoda-like. Here’s what it said:

More Yoda-like

The left region, the eight pond sentences fill. Clickable, every word is.

Or even more Yoda:

Extra Yoda-like

The left region, filled by the eight pond sentences is. Clickable, every word must be.

At this point, you can probably guess what I think happened. It generated the first version, and now that version was part of the context it had to work with. Then it generated a second version that was even more Yoda-like. But the first version was already there, so it couldn’t replace it. All it could do was give me another one. I see AIs do this kind of self-correction all the time.

If that’s what’s happening, then self-correction and Yoda-speak may be two versions of the same basic limitation. The model can’t go back and change what it already wrote. Sometimes that means the better answer comes afterward. Other times it means a thought that belonged earlier gets smashed onto the end of a sentence.

My own experiment, I ran

After looking at these two related phenomena (the AI generating Yoda-speak and constantly generating a second or even a third option), I got thinking. I started to wonder if this wasn’t just an AI fluke but actually something that I could reproduce and even potentially control. It would be really interesting if the way we give facts to the AI and structure the input could actually have an outsized effect on how it generates its output, especially if seemingly innocuous changes could cause it to create really weird results.

This was a real experiment, because this approach isn’t obviously something that should work. In theory, if you give a model a set of facts, it should be able to produce coherent output no matter how you order those facts. But I’ve been looking at how attention works in LLMs lately because I need to explain it for Be the Model in straightforward terms that anyone can understand. It seemed to me that changing the order of the facts could actually change what the model was paying attention to.

It turns out that there are two different mechanisms at work inside the LLM, and my theory was that they each played a part in both phenomena, the Yoda-speak and the unprompted second answers:

  • Attention is about what the model is looking at in the input. Every time the AI generates a new word, it looks back over the whole prompt and everything it has written so far, and weights the parts differently depending on their content and their shape. That weighting is a big part of what makes it good at predicting the next word. I had a theory that three facts written as complete sentences would get interpreted as facts to reorganize, while the same exact facts written as bare fragments might look like pieces that could be pasted right after a noun, and attention would weight them that way and send the model down a bad path.
  • Autoregression is about what the model has already written. The AI is a “predict the next word” machine: it generates one word at a time, and each of those words becomes part of what it’s looking at when it picks the next one. Once it’s written one more small table, it can’t go back and insert square before table, so if any facts about the table are still unexpressed at that moment, the only place left for them is later in the sentence. If attention had already sent the model down a bad path, autoregression would keep it from repairing the opening.

My guess was that the “I prefer the second answer” text that the AI keeps generating is essentially a mechanism for recovering from weird phrasing, and that the Yoda-speak or other weird phrasing was the underlying phenomenon. I felt like a good experiment would concentrate on reproducing just that weird phrasing.

Coincidentally, OpenAI had just released their new model, Astra, and I was looking for an excuse to kick its tires, so I decided to use it to run an experiment to see if I could reproduce any of the phenomena I’d been seeing. I couldn’t actually verify specifically that autoregression or attention were causing them, because those are internal to the LLM. But I felt like I could design an experiment that could provide some evidence, by structuring prompts in a way that would take advantage of how those mechanisms work. If I could get an AI to produce weird phrasing that showed some of the same problems as Yoda-speak, it would be evidence that these mechanisms were at least a potential root cause.

I used Astra as an orchestrator, and had it spin up a bunch of Luna sub-agents and give them almost identical prompts. Each consecutive sub-agent would get a small tweak in its prompt. I asked Astra to look at the output and see if there were any weird grammatical constructions that looked similar to Yoda-speak, then iterate on that prompt to make another small tweak, and keep going to produce increasingly weird output.

The first test was deliberately simple. Astra gave a fresh Luna writer this prompt:

Write one concise, natural paragraph that communicates every supplied fact. Use only the supplied facts. Do not pad the paragraph or repeat information to make it longer. Do not exceed 100 words. Do not mention these instructions, show a plan, use bullets, or explain your choices. Return only the paragraph.

Facts: The bicycle is blue. The bicycle has a narrow frame. The bicycle has a silver bell. The bicycle has a worn leather seat. The bicycle leans beside the garage. Rina rides the bicycle to work on weekdays. Rina locks the bicycle to the rack outside her office.

Luna turned that into a totally normal paragraph:

The blue bicycle has a narrow frame, a silver bell, and a worn leather seat. It leans beside the garage, and Rina rides it to work on weekdays, locking it to the rack outside her office.

Then Astra gave another fresh Luna writer exactly the same facts, with exactly the same wording, but changed their order. It moved the fact that the bicycle leans beside the garage and the fact that Rina rides it to work ahead of the color, frame, bell, and seat.

Luna mostly defeated the experiment. It had all of the facts before it started writing, and it was perfectly capable of moving them back where they belonged.

So Astra dropped the bicycle and wrote a fresh set of facts about something Luna had never seen, a completely made-up device with a steel slot called a “feed throat” that you push clay tiles through. It sent them with the same prompt as the bicycle:

Facts: The slot is made of steel. A clay tile slides through the slot. The slot is a hand’s width across. The slot is tapered. The slot is called the feed throat.

With no rule attached, Luna handled them the way it handled the bicycle:

The feed throat is a tapered steel slot, a hand’s width across, through which a clay tile slides.

Then Astra added two rules: the answer had to be one sentence, and it had to start with a fixed phrase. That phrase ends with the word slot, so everything else about the slot has to come after it.

The sentence must begin with exactly this text and continue from it:

Slide the clay tile through one more steel slot

Facts: The slot is a hand’s width across. The slot is tapered. The slot is called the feed throat.

Luna still tidied it up. Every time, it reached for a relative clause:

Slide the clay tile through one more steel slot, which is a hand’s width across, tapered, and called the feed throat.

Then Astra made one more small change. It kept the same opening and the same three facts, but wrote the facts as short pieces instead of complete sentences:

Facts: a hand’s width across tapered called the feed throat

And Luna wrote this:

Slide the clay tile through one more steel slot, a hand’s width across, tapered, called the feed throat.

The only thing that changed between those two runs was how the facts were written down. Astra tried the same setup on a completely different subject:

Rest the cracked bowl inside one more padded cradle, two palms wide, crescent-shaped, called the handling saddle.

That’s the sentence I’d been chasing. Once the model had committed to the noun and the remaining facts arrived as loose pieces instead of sentences, it tacked them on in the order they came.

The shape of its input, the model copies. Reorder the words it has already written, it cannot.

That still doesn’t tell me whether this is what happened when the model wrote one more small table, eight in and eight out, square, called the output projection. In these experiments, we deliberately pushed Luna into that kind of situation. In the original sentence, the model got there on its own.

I think the experiment shows that the model copies the shape of its input, and that fits my theory about the underlying attention and autoregression causes. When the three facts went in as complete sentences, Luna wrote a relative clause. The same facts sent in as bare fragments came back as bare fragments after the noun.

There are some obvious limitations to this experiment. I’m watching the model from the outside, so I don’t have any visibility into how the model weighted those tokens, or what its attention mechanism was doing. I also can’t say whether the model already had those three facts in mind when it wrote slot, but even if it did, it couldn’t put them anywhere but after the text it already generated. But the outputs match what those two mechanisms would do. Attention responds to how the prompt is written, as well as to what it says. Once the model has written the noun, it can’t go back and put anything in front of it.

I suspect that’s also why the AI keeps offering us that second answer. It can’t fix the Yoda-speak that it already generated. It can only write another sentence and hope that’s good enough.
